transcript.text: Hi, I'm Sensei. Put your page under the camera and start solving. I'm watching.
You wrote v_y = 20 m/s, but the ball was launched at 60 degrees—what part of the velocity is vertical?
I don't get it. It's going 20 meters per second, isn't that the speed going up?
Okay, let me think.
The 20 m/s is the total speed, not the vertical part. What part of the velocity is vertical when launched at 60 degrees?
I don't know what you mean by part of the velocity. How does a speed have parts?
Good question. One moment.

Good question—speed is the total, but velocity has parts. Think of it like a triangle: the total speed is the hypotenuse, and the vertical part is one side. What trig function gives the opposite side?
Sine is opposite over hypotenuse. But I don't get which side is the opposite one here.
Let me see.
Yes, sine gives opposite over hypotenuse. In this case, the vertical part is opposite the 60-degree angle, so v_y = 20 m/s × sin(60°).
Oh, so the angle is at the bottom from the ground, and up is across from it. So v_y is 20 sin 60, like 17.3?
Got it. Give me a second.
You're on the right track with the angle, but v_y isn't 20 m/s—what's the correct way to find the vertical part?
Wait, I said 20 times sin 60, which is 17.3. Is that not right?
Okay, let me think.
You're right that v_y = 20 m/s × sin(60°), but you wrote v_y = 20 m/s, which is the total speed, not the vertical part. Try again with the correct expression.
Okay so I cross out 20 and put v_y equals 17.3. Then time is 2 times 17.3 over 9.8, so about 3.54 seconds. Thanks.
Good question. One moment.
Yes, you fixed it—v_y is 20 m/s times sin(60°), not 20 m/s. Now write that down and keep going.
